newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank says depreciation trend limited.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank says depreciation trend limited.

text.p: Central bank deputy governor Hsu Chia-tung said on Friday that the Taiwan dollar's recent depreciation was a "limited" trend caused chiefly by a net US$500 million outflow of foreign capital in May.
"If there is no outflow interference, the room for depreciation of the Taiwan dollar is limited," Hsu told reporters after the close of trading.

Hsu said there had been an average daily outflow of several tens of millions of U.S. dollars during May, and that the entire month saw a net outflow of about US$500 million, which had pushed the local currency lower.
A short time later, after checking his figures, Hsu corrected himself to say the net ouflow had been closer to "US$300 million to US$400 million" rather than his earlier half-billion dollar figure.

Analysts have attributed the big May outflow to repatriation of profits earned by foreign equity funds in Taiwan's stock market, which surged by some 25 percent in the first four months of 1997 before entering a consolidation that only recently has begun to ease.
The Taiwan dollar continued its recent downward trend to close at an eight-year low on Friday.

The dollar flirted with the central bank's T$27.9 defense level throughout the session -- trading at or below that level for hours before firming to finish at T$27.896 against Thursday's T$27.890 close. The Taiwan dollar has not closed lower since its T$28.03 finish on January 7, 1989.

The Taiwan dollar has been on a long, slow decline since mid-January and recently has repeatedly flirted with T$27.9, prompting dealers to predict it would break support at T$28 in the second half -- but not until the central bank is ready.
Dealers said Hsu's comment reflected the central bank's basic policy of not wanting the Taiwan dollar to drop below the T$27.90 support level.
"It's pretty obvious the central bank is using the psychological approach -- Hsu's comment -- to stop the dollar from going down further," a dealer of a foreign bank said.

The central bank defended the dollar at T$27.5 through the 1990s but said in mid-1996 it was abandoning the policy, hinting a depreciation was welcome in the interest of stronger exports to help accelerate a stubbornly sluggish recovery.
"Just as in the past few days, the market continued to test T$27.90 but the central bank's defence was almost unbeatable," said another dealer at a foreign bank.
Dealers said they expected the trend of slow depreciation would not change in the near term.

In a May 30 Reuters Poll of senior Taipei dealers, four of six dealers said Taiwan's easing dollar was likely to break eight-year support at T$28 in the third quarter, citing slack economic growth and political uncertainties.
All six cautioned that the central bank was determined to defend the Taiwan dollar's stability to prevent an acceleration of capital outflows that would hurt Taiwan people's confidence.
Two of the six said the central bank's defence would be so strenuous that the dollar would only approach -- but not break -- the T$28 level.
